conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling during the past seven days so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve in this postpartum period.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience. We’ll move through the questions at your pace; each one just asks how often you’ve felt a certain way.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

First question: Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Most of the time I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as I used to, but usually once a day something the baby does or my husband says will make me crack a smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… like I said, I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced sometimes—almost like I’m pretending to enjoy the moment more than I really do.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not very often. Even when I plan something small—like meeting a friend for coffee—I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point?” I still go, and once I’m there I can feel a little spark, but it’s nowhere near the excitement I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m failing him somehow. I know rationally it’s not all on me, but the guilty voice in my head keeps saying I should be better at this mom thing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Almost every day. I’ll be sitting there, everything quiet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure the baby’s too hot or his breathing sounds weird. Even when the doctor says he’s fine, I can’t shake the thought that something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though I can’t name what. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, it’s already time for the next, and the laundry and dishes just keep piling up. I’ll look around the house and think, “I can’t keep up,” and my chest gets heavy. I usually manage to push through, but it’s overwhelming more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Several nights this week. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is the baby breathing, am I already a bad mom. It can take an hour or two to drift off, and then I wake up at 2 a.m. with the same thoughts racing.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… pretty much every day. It’s not crying-all-day sad, just this heavy, gray feeling that sits on me. I’ll be holding the baby and still feel empty, like I’m watching myself from outside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t settle for almost an hour and I felt totally useless; the other time was after my mom left and the house felt so quiet and I just sat on the couch and sobbed for a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It flashed through my mind a couple of times—like a quick picture of what if I just didn’t wake up—but I shoved it away right after. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it; it just popped in, scared me, and left me feeling guilty for even thinking it.

You've shared that over the past week most moments feel heavy and gray; laughter comes only with effort, excitement for get-togethers is almost gone, and you often feel you're failing your baby even when you rationally know you're doing your best. Nights are restless with racing worries, sudden surges of panic arrive out of nowhere, and twice you've broken into tears. Fleeting thoughts of not waking up have popped in, scaring you and leaving guilt behind. You push through feedings and chores, but a sense of being overwhelmed lingers most of the day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to enjoy humor, describing laughter as forced and inauthentic, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports enjoying planned events "nowhere near" previous levels, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('happens a lot') tied to routine infant care, indicating this occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about the baby despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic symptoms that occur "sometimes," matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and describes persistent daily stress, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty on several nights, taking 1-2 hours to fall asleep and waking at 2 a.m. with racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad or miserable "pretty much every day" with a persistent "heavy, gray feeling" and emotional emptiness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 22 places you well above the 14-point threshold that flags probable major depression; item 10 (self-harm) scored 1, meeting safety-alert criteria. Daily <sym>sad mood</sym>, near-daily <sym>loss of interest</sym>, multiple <sym>guilt episodes</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic spells</sym>, and <sym>sleep difficulty</sym> align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week review with your <med>GP</med>, midwife, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Ask about starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or, if indicated, <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Complete a written safety plan now: list 24-h support numbers, emergency contacts, and coping activities
4. Share these EPDS results and your <sym>transient self-harm thoughts</sym> with a trusted partner or family member so they can stay close and help monitor mood
5. Prioritise 2-3 h total daily rest broken into short naps; accept household help to reduce workload
6. Plan daily 15-min outdoor walk or gentle stroller outing; sunlight and mild exercise can ease <sym>low mood</sym>
7. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after supports are in place
8. If thoughts of self-harm intensify or plans develop, attend A&E or call local emergency services immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (2 wks postpartum):
- Depressed mood, daily “heavy, gray feeling,” episodic crying
- Marked anhedonia; anticipatory enjoyment absent, in-the-moment pleasure blunted
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care
- Persistent, ill-defined anxiety and situational panic symptoms (physical arousal, catastrophic worries about infant safety)
- Sleep-onset and mid-night awakening directly linked to ruminating worries
- Sense of being overwhelmed by routine infant/household demands
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation (no plan, intent, or preparatory behavior) — safety concern documented

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, causing subjective distress and functional difficulty, consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in the postpartum period.

Risk flags: Guilt, anhedonia, sleep disruption tied to mood, passive suicidal thoughts.

Recommendation: Continue to full diagnostic assessment; evaluate for safety plan and appropriate level of care.
